note: Rabbi Shimon recalled that in the village of Pani an old man asked him whether Rabbi Akiva really held that sprinkling the blood takes effect even for sacrificial meat that had left the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Shimon said yes. When he reported this to his colleagues in Galilee, they asked how sprinkling could count for meat that was already unfit. He then put the matter to Rabbi Akiva, who said, my son, do you not hold so yourself, and began to argue from the case of a sin offering that was lost, replaced, and then found. The rest of his argument is not given here.
why: The Gemara has been examining Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling the blood frees meat that left the courtyard from the laws of misuse, and Rabbi Elazar's limit on it. Rabbi Shimon's account is the source of Rabbi Akiva's comparison to the lost and found sin offering.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's student, who carries a question about his teacher's view from Pani to Galilee and back to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva

note: In Rome, Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash asked Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai how we know creeping animals' blood is impure, and got a verse. He told his admiring students it was Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's tradition, and told why: Rome had forbidden Shabbat and circumcision. Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobeli, passing as a gentile, talked them out of each decree, but once they saw he was a Jew they restored them. The Sages sent Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai with Rabbi Elazar. On the road Rabbi Elazar whispered that verse in his teacher's presence, and Rabbi Shimon cursed him never to return to his father. The demon ben Temalyon possessed the emperor's daughter; Rabbi Shimon drove it out, and in the emperor's treasury they found the decree and tore it up.
why: The Gemara has been discussing when blood joins with flesh to make up a measure for impurity. The story is attached because it records where the teaching that creeping animals' blood is impure comes from.
